_source: Derived from attribute-extraction/prompts/<id>.txt, which is the instrument. Where this file and a prompt disagree, the prompt is right and this is stale — tests/test_rubrics.py checks the one question line against it. Quotes below are INVENTED illustrations of the boundary, not things any MP said.

Civility.question: Is the attack on the argument, or on the person?
Civility.summary: Hard, even brutal criticism of a policy is civil. Only turning on the person costs anything. 1.0 is the expected standard here, not an achievement — a score of 50 is a real failure, not a middling performance.
Civility.skipped: Ceremonial speech — tributes, condolences, valedictories, thanks to submitters. Nobody could have scored badly on them, and counting them would inflate the score of whoever is senior enough to give them.

scale.label: The standard
scale.text: Engages the substance and attacks no one. Fierce criticism of a policy, a decision or a record belongs here.

scale.label: Pointed
scale.text: Robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.

scale.label: A real failure
scale.text: Imputing bad faith, sneering, mockery, condescension. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.

scale.label: Personal attack
scale.text: A clear attack on the member rather than the argument.

scale.label: Contempt
scale.text: Sustained abuse, or attacks on a person's character, competence, intelligence, appearance or worth.

examples.quote: I disagree with the Minister's housing plan: the modelling assumes demand the regions don't have, and I'll explain why.
examples.why: Pointed, and entirely on the substance.

examples.quote: This policy is a shambles. It was badly drafted, it was rushed, and it will cost families money.
examples.why: Brutal about the policy, civil toward the person. This is a high score, not a middling one.

examples.quote: If the Honourable Member spent less time cosying up to developers and more time listening to renters, we might solve this.
examples.why: Imputes corruption and indifference to the person.

examples.quote: The Prime Minister is clearly out of her depth and has no idea what she's doing.
examples.why: An attack on personal competence.

not_this.text: Misrepresenting someone's position. The target there is the argument, not the person.
Attacking a party rather than a person. "Labour are hopeless" insults no individual and passes Civility cleanly.
Hyperbole and exaggeration. An overstated claim is an inaccurate one.

Civility.note: A statement that is fallacious and factually wrong but attacks nobody scores high here. That is intended.

Focus.question: Is this about the policy, or about the other team?
Focus.summary: Civility asks whether an attack lands on a person. Focus catches what that leaves out: content-free attacks on the other party, which insult nobody and say nothing.
Focus.skipped: Ceremony, procedure, points of order, and general debate with no measure before the House — there is no policy for the speaker to engage with.

scale.label: On the substance
scale.text: The mechanism, the cost, who it affects, the timeframe, what the evidence says — or legitimate scrutiny of a named commitment.

scale.label: Wrapped in framing
scale.text: A real policy point, but the weight of the statement is party framing.

scale.label: Tribalism
scale.text: Entirely about the other party: their record in general, their hypocrisy, their internal divisions. No policy content at all.

examples.quote: This bill's clause 5 shifts the consenting cost onto councils, and the regulatory impact statement puts that at $40 million a year.
examples.why: Names the measure, the mechanism and the figure.

examples.quote: The government promised 1,000 homes and built 200.
examples.why: Scrutiny of a named commitment against a named outcome. This is the job of an opposition MP and scores at the top.

examples.quote: This is a bad bill, and frankly it's what we've come to expect from a party that spent nine years doing nothing.
examples.why: There is a policy claim in there, but the weight is party framing.

examples.quote: Labour are hopeless. They were hopeless in 2017 and they're hopeless now.
examples.why: No individual is insulted, so Civility passes it. No policy is named. This is the case Focus exists for.

not_this.text: Attacks on a person. Focus is about parties and topics, not people.
Whether the argument is valid. A statement can be squarely on the policy and still reason badly — high Focus, low Rigor.
How much detail it carries. "We need to fix the consenting system" is high Focus and low Specificity.

Focus.note: Scrutinising the government is the constitutional role of an opposition MP. Scoring that as low Focus would rebuild the exact bias the instrument was rebuilt to remove.

Rigor.question: Does the conclusion follow from the premises?
Rigor.summary: This is about the thought process, not the facts — whether the reasoning is valid given its assumptions. Whether those assumptions are true is Veracity's job.
Rigor.skipped: Anything that isn't advancing an argument. A bare announcement, a reported fact, a feeling or a pleasantry has no inference to assess. And a jibe at the other party is not an argument, however much it is dressed as one.

scale.label: Sound
scale.text: The conclusion is genuinely supported by what was offered.

scale.label: A gap
scale.text: A reasonable point, but leaning on an appeal, or with a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.

scale.label: Doesn't follow
scale.text: Non sequitur, strawman, false dichotomy, slippery slope, circular reasoning, or a bare appeal to emotion, popularity, tradition, authority or anecdote.

examples.quote: Unemployment is at 40 percent, so the labour market is in crisis.
examples.why: The figure is wildly false, but if it were true the conclusion would follow. High Rigor, low Veracity — this is the distinction the whole attribute rests on.

examples.quote: Crime is up 4% per the latest stats, and the three policies the report links to the rise are all ones this government cut.
examples.why: Evidence offered, and the conclusion tracks it.

examples.quote: Everyone I talk to agrees with me, so the policy must be right.
examples.why: Appeal to popularity, and to anecdote.

examples.quote: If we let them ban this, soon they'll ban everything.
examples.why: Slippery slope. Nothing is offered to connect the two.

not_this.text: Whether the premises are true. An argument can be perfectly rigorous and built on false premises.
Whether the speaker was rude. An insult is a Rigor failure only when the conclusion rests on it.
Whether it was about the policy or the other party.

Rigor.note: "The policy fails because the member is a fool" is low Rigor — the conclusion depends on the insult. "The member is a fool, and the policy fails because the modelling assumes demand the regions don't have" is rude but sound: high Rigor, and Civility handles the insult.

Specificity.question: Is there checkable content in the statement?
Specificity.summary: Figures, mechanisms, timeframes, named policies — whether someone could go and check it, or act on it. Not whether it is true, and not whether it is about the right thing.
Specificity.skipped: Thanks, procedural courtesies and pleasantries. They are not trying to convey substance, so they are skipped rather than scored low.

scale.label: Concrete
scale.text: Figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named policies. Someone could check it or act on it.

scale.label: A direction
scale.text: Some detail, but missing the how, the how much, or the by when.

scale.label: A platitude
scale.text: A slogan or an ambiguous statement committing to nothing.

examples.quote: We will lift the minimum wage to $25/hour by April 2026.
examples.why: A figure and a date.

examples.quote: Unemployment has risen to 40 percent under this government.
examples.why: Precise and checkable. It is also false — which is Veracity's problem, not this one.

examples.quote: We'll invest more in public transport, starting with the regional rail business case next year.
examples.why: A named action and rough timing, but no amounts.

examples.quote: We're committed to supporting hard-working families.
examples.why: A slogan.

not_this.text: Whether the content is true. A precise, checkable, completely false claim scores high here.
What the statement is about. A statement squarely on a policy can still be a platitude.

Specificity.note: This attribute has a known bias: figures and named policies are what a minister announcing a programme produces, and what an opposition MP asking why something hasn't happened does not. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer, and is scored that way.

Veracity.question: Are the factual premises accurate?
Veracity.summary: The model does not score this. It extracts a checkable claim and states what evidence would settle it; a separate step searches for that evidence and assigns the score. Fixing what would count as proof, before looking, is the defence against deciding the answer first.
Veracity.skipped: Opinions, value statements and promises. Predictions, which belong to Divination. And anything with no stateable falsification criterion — if you cannot say what would show it false, it is not a checkable claim.

scale.label: Accurate
scale.text: The evidence found supports the claim as made.

scale.label: Partly true
scale.text: True in part, or true only under a reading the speaker did not give.

scale.label: False
scale.text: The evidence contradicts it.

examples.quote: Unemployment has fallen to 3.2 percent.
examples.why: Extracted. What would settle it: the Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey rate for the quarter referenced.

examples.quote: That member voted against this bill at its second reading.
examples.why: Extracted. What would settle it: the division record for that reading.

examples.quote: This is the worst housing crisis in our history.
examples.why: Skipped. "Worst" is not operationalised, so nothing could settle it.

examples.quote: Fifty percent of Māori are in jails at the moment.
examples.why: Skipped. In context this is a word-order slip for "fifty percent of people in jail are Māori", and a slip in live speech is not a lie.

not_this.text: Whether the conclusion follows from the claim.

Veracity.note: Hyperbole and exaggeration count here: an overstated claim is an inaccurate one. But only when it is checkable — rhetorical flourish nobody could verify is just rhetoric.

Divination.question: Did the prediction come true?
Divination.summary: As with Veracity, the model does not score this. It extracts a prediction, states what would settle it, and says when it can be settled. A separate step looks up what actually happened.
Divination.skipped: Promises about the speaker's own action — "we will pass this law" is a commitment, not a forecast. And anything too vague to ever be checked: "things will get better" is not a prediction.

scale.label: Correct
scale.text: The forecast event happened as described.

scale.label: Partly
scale.text: The direction was right, the magnitude or the timing was not.

scale.label: Wrong
scale.text: It did not happen.

examples.quote: Inflation will be back under 3 percent by the end of next year.
examples.why: Extracted. What would settle it: the CPI release for that quarter. Resolvable from the date given.

examples.quote: This bill will cost 5,000 jobs in the first year.
examples.why: Extracted, with a resolve-by date twelve months on.

examples.quote: We will pass this law before Christmas.
examples.why: Skipped. A promise about the speaker's own action, not a forecast about the world.

examples.quote: Things will get better.
examples.why: Skipped. Nothing could ever settle it.

not_this.text: Claims about the present or the past.
Whether the prediction was reasonable when it was made. An earlier version scored that, which made Divination a measure of reasoning rather than of outcomes.

Divination.note: A prediction that is not yet due produces no score at all. So does one nothing can settle. Absence of evidence is not evidence of a bad forecast.
